title: Educating an Architect: A Conversation with Luca Mezzalira
gist: In an InfoQ Architects Podcast interview by Michael Stiefel, Luca Mezzalira (ex-DAZN VP of Architecture, ex-AWS) argues architecture is a socio-technical discipline, that architects should become enablement coaches setting guardrails and fitness functions, and that AI delegation should be calibrated by DDD subdomain: heavy human oversight on core domains, more AI autonomy on generic ones like payments. He warns the agentic wave is forgetting software fundamentals such as security, and argues pair/mob programming is the answer to training juniors when AI writes the code.

insights.claim: Mezzalira uses domain-driven design subdomain types to decide how much human-in-the-loop to apply to AI coding: core domains need heavy human oversight, supporting domains allow more delegation, and generic domains can be largely delegated to AI.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Gives enterprises a risk-tiering model for where AI coding productivity gains can safely be captured.
insights.quote: leveraging domain-driven design, sub-domains type, in order to decide how much human in the loop I want to have
insights.locator: So I believe we are still trying

insights.claim: Using Netflix as an example, the video player and catalog are core domains needing human-in-the-loop care, personalization is a supporting domain where outages are tolerable, and payments via Stripe or Zuora SDKs is a generic domain with no differentiation suitable for AI delegation.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Commodity integration work like payments is the most exposed to AI automation.
insights.locator: So if it's a core domain

insights.claim: Code volatility and rate of change in core domains are key signals for where humans must retain full control over AI-generated code.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: High-change differentiating code remains a human-labor stronghold.
insights.quote: This is probably a high rate of change, so code volatility is important.
insights.locator: This is probably a high rate

insights.claim: Small, low-traffic projects (e.g. 10 requests per second) barely need design and could be built by agents, but mid-size and large organizations have years of hidden context in documents and people's heads that agents cannot access.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: AI may replace architecture work in the long tail of small software but not in large enterprises.
insights.quote: when you are in mid-size, large organizations, there is a lot of context that is hidden over the years
insights.locator: I think agents are a very interesting tool

insights.claim: Agents are constrained by token limits, context-window limits and summarization limits, and are probabilistic systems that usually but not always recommend the right thing, so tech, product and business must still align on what is being built.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Human alignment work remains a bottleneck that limits pure AI-driven development.
insights.locator: Sometimes in documents, sometimes in people’s heads

insights.claim: At QCon London two opposing approaches were presented: delegating everything to AI and focusing on input/output, versus augmenting the existing SDLC with AI; the former demands trust while the latter yields perhaps 2X rather than 10X gains.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Realistic productivity uplift from AI-augmented development may be closer to 2X than 10X.
insights.quote: we move the needle not 10X, but maybe 2X
insights.locator: I think currently we are testing it out.

insights.claim: AWS proposed an AI-DLC with 'bolts' to replace practices like Scrum and two-week sprints, arguing the traditional SDLC was designed for humans.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Signals vendors repositioning development methodology around agents.
insights.locator: And it really resonated with me

insights.claim: Gas Town, an agent orchestrator, has a creator who claims never to have looked at the code it produced, treating speed as more important than perfection, while Mezzalira notes well-known applications are starting to show bugs never seen before.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Fully autonomous coding may be degrading software quality, a risk for vendors and users of AI-built software.
insights.locator: We have seen a Gas Town

insights.claim: A QCon keynote message that resonated with Mezzalira is that everyone is a junior in the AI revolution regardless of experience.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Expertise advantage is temporarily flattened, accelerating experimentation.
insights.quote: We are all juniors in this new revolution despite your level of expertise or experience
insights.locator: I think currently we are testing it out.

insights.claim: Mezzalira contrasts the architecture community's balanced view of AI with a 'fanboy approach' elsewhere that claims everything can be done with AI, arguing that being able to do something does not mean you should.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Expect a backlash/correction narrative against maximalist AI coding claims.
insights.quote: Absolutely, you can do everything with anything, but doesn't mean that because you can, you should.
insights.locator: I've seen these more balanced approaches

themes.theme: Security and fundamentals in the agentic wave

insights.claim: The agentic revolution began with MCP lacking authentication, and Mezzalira cannot recall any previous game-changing API or technique that so completely ignored security.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Agent security is an underbuilt layer, implying demand for agent security and governance tooling.
insights.quote: we started with the MCP that didn't have any authentication
insights.locator: Sometimes in documents, sometimes in people’s heads

insights.claim: Attacks are occurring through open-source packages and through people installing agents on their computers with access to credit cards and email, showing software fundamentals are being forgotten.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Supply-chain and agent-permission attacks are a growing risk vector.
insights.locator: Now, I don't recall any game changer

insights.claim: Mezzalira believes AI will augment architects and humans rather than fully replace every role today, freeing more time for thinking.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Supports an augmentation rather than substitution view of AI impact on senior engineering labor.
insights.locator: And that's why I believe that architects

insights.claim: Companies are rushing to replace HR and customer support with AI, and large organizations are cutting the smallest departments even when they are key, which reveals the current C-suite mindset.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: AI-driven headcount cuts are targeting small support functions first.
insights.quote: So that probably tells you already where the mindset of the C-suite is at the moment.
insights.locator: This is probably a high rate

insights.claim: The interviewer Michael Stiefel proposed that every agent should check a governance table to confirm it has not been turned off, so rogue agents can always be shut down, and Mezzalira agreed.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Kill-switch governance for agents is emerging as a baseline control.
insights.locator: You don't actually want to have an AI agent

insights.claim: Architects should evolve into enablement teams akin to security, since organizations typically have roughly one security architect per 20 developers and one architect every two teams would make costs surge.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Architecture headcount is likely to shrink in favor of decentralized decision-making with guardrails.
insights.quote: You cannot have let's say one architect every two teams because the cost will surge drastically.
insights.locator: Luca Mezzalira: To be honest with you

insights.claim: Mezzalira endorses Andrew Harmel-Law's architecture advice process, where anyone can design but a fluid group of API consumers and experts reviews designs and sets direction.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Decentralized governance models are replacing formal architecture review boards.
insights.locator: Andrew Harmel-Law discussed this part

insights.claim: Fully decentralized design struggles with the two-to-five cross-domain features per year, because team members are biased toward their own domain and promotion incentives reward local wins.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Holistic roles remain necessary for cross-cutting initiatives in 50-100+ person orgs.
insights.quote: The gamification of promotions in general in every single company
insights.locator: But thinking about being an architect as a coach

insights.claim: Architects should own the holistic view, build architectural fitness functions and guardrails, and surface patterns across teams rather than just designing.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Automated architecture governance tooling becomes more valuable as design decentralizes.
insights.locator: Building Architectural Fitness Functions

insights.claim: At DAZN, Mezzalira told his team that 70% of the architect role is empathy with the people they work with and 30% is being technical.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Communication is a core, not soft, skill for technical leaders in the AI era.
insights.quote: 70% of your role is being empathic with the people that you need to work with and 30% is being technical
insights.locator: I feel that we need to do more

insights.claim: Developers carry growing load from shift-left of DevOps, security, architecture and code, which AI only partly offsets by taking over some code creation.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Developer cognitive load, not coding time, may be the binding constraint on AI productivity.
insights.locator: Now maybe with AI we can delegate

insights.claim: Communication should be treated as a core skill rather than a soft skill, especially as AI makes code creation easier and leaves more time for design and alignment.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Value of engineers shifts from code output toward communication and system thinking.
insights.locator: Elevating Communication from a Soft Skill

insights.claim: Architectural choices like microservices versus monolith should be adapted to organizational culture and team structure rather than universal best practices, as Conway's law implies systems mirror communication structures.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Vendor narratives about 'the right architecture' should be discounted against org context.
insights.locator: Understanding Socio-Technical Systems

insights.claim: A conference speaker who blamed microservices and moved to a monolith had gone from five teams with ten microservices to one team, a context omitted from the talk that explained the decision.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Public 'back to monolith' stories often reflect team shrinkage, not architectural failure.
insights.quote: before we were five teams and we have 10 microservices and now we are just one team and we have a monolith
insights.locator: We also need to understand the context.

insights.claim: Spotify never actually implemented its famous squad model as designed, and copying it ignores that Spotify's engineering culture is unique.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Org-model imitation of big tech firms carries hidden failure risk.
insights.locator: Oh yes, we are using Squad like Spotify

insights.claim: Friction within a system is feedback signaling misalignment between technical design and team structures, and the fix may be redesigning teams rather than the architecture.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Reorgs can be as effective as rewrites for resolving delivery friction.
insights.locator: Friction, I always interpret as a gift

insights.claim: Customers who ask for 'near real time' data often mean anything from one minute to one hour, and probing context reveals teams optimizing for requirements no one asked for, creating avoidable complexity.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Requirement discovery can cut infrastructure cost and complexity materially.
insights.locator: And this discovery of the context

insights.claim: Pair and mob programming, cited via Kent Beck, are more important than ever for growing junior developers when AI handles easy tasks, with two-person PR reviews of AI code enabling asynchronous learning.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Firms that keep apprenticeship practices will preserve their talent pipeline as AI absorbs junior tasks.
insights.locator: I'm with you on this one.

insights.claim: The interviewer cited a study (Shen & Tamkin) in which developers learning with AI progressed at the same pace as a control group but had significantly less retention afterwards.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: AI-assisted learning may erode skill formation, a long-term workforce risk.
insights.locator: Well, your safe deposit box is not quite

insights.claim: Mezzalira is encouraged that many companies are still hiring juniors and expects the community to figure out how to train them in the AI era.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Junior hiring collapse fears may be overstated.
insights.locator: In general, I believe, yes, it's a challenge

insights.claim: A RAG system over how a team works on a product could let new hires onboard faster than before.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Internal knowledge-assistant tools have an onboarding use case.
insights.locator: And I think we can potentially even accelerate

insights.claim: At Gamesys, a real-money gambling company, Mezzalira's move to a simpler framework cut game development time from nine months to three months per game.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Simplification of tooling can triple delivery throughput.
insights.quote: So we moved from nine months to three months for each single game.
insights.locator: I was a tech leader of a real money

insights.claim: DAZN's micro-frontend architecture designed by Mezzalira was still unchanged after eight years, according to its principal engineers.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Well-modularized architectures can have very long useful lives.
insights.locator: We didn't change anything about your architecture

insights.claim: Mezzalira's previous company moved from VMs to serverless on AWS Lambda starting in 2015, serving three to four million customers with huge traffic spikes using Lambda plus Fargate containers, and he considers serverless scale problems largely solved for many use cases.
insights.speaker: Luca Mezzalira
insights.so_what: Serverless is mature for large consumer platforms with spiky traffic.
insights.locator: Yes, I do, obviously, as everyone
